title: Hunter Valley
description: Australia's oldest wine region: humid and hot, yet home to unoaked Sémillon that ages magically.
L: The Hunter Valley lies about 160 km north of Sydney, in New South Wales, along the Hunter River. It's divided into the Lower Hunter, around Pokolbin, the main wine area, and the Upper Hunter. It has about 2,500 hectares of vines. Soils include sandy alluvial flats, good for Sémillon, and red clay on slopes, for Shiraz.

The Hunter is one of Australia's hottest, most humid wine regions, and unusually, much rain falls in summer and at harvest, from February to March. Afternoon cloud and sea breezes moderate the heat. The risk of rot at harvest is high, so grapes are often picked early. It's a challenging, sub-tropical climate for vines.
What is unusual about the Hunter's rainfall?
Much of it falls in summer and at harvest

The Hunter is Australia's oldest continuously operating wine region. James Busby, the father of Australian wine, planted vines there in the 1820s and brought hundreds of cuttings from Europe in 1832. Families like Tyrrell, Tulloch and McWilliam's, with Mount Pleasant, have made wine for generations.
The Hunter Valley is Australia's oldest wine region still in operation.
The Hunter lies north of Sydney, around Pokolbin
It's hot and humid, with rain at harvest

Hunter Sémillon is picked early, at about 10 to 11% alcohol, to avoid harvest rain and keep acidity. It's fermented cool in steel, without oak or malolactic, and bottled early. Young, it's pale, lean and lemony, with grass and high acidity. With 5 to 10 years in bottle, it transforms, gaining toast, honey, lanolin and lemon curd, as if oaked.
Picked early, unoaked, transforms with age

Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied, unlike the Barossa's, with red fruit, earth and a savoury, leathery character, sometimes called sweaty saddle in older wines. It's lower in alcohol, around 13 to 13.5%, and ages well. Chardonnay is also grown. Tyrrell's Vat 1 Sémillon and Vat 9 Shiraz are famous examples.
Match each term to the Hunter.
The Hunter's grapes have a distinct style.
Hunter Sémillon's toasty notes after ten years come entirely from bottle age, not oak. It's one of wine's great transformations.
Why is Hunter Sémillon picked so early?
To avoid harvest rain and keep acidity
Early picking avoids rot and preserves freshness.
Hunter Sémillon is picked early, unoaked, and transforms with age
Hunter Shiraz is medium-bodied and earthy
Tyrrell's Vat 1 and Vat 9 are famous examples
Reading the Hunter and eating with it

Labels show the grape, Hunter Valley GI, sometimes Lower Hunter or Pokolbin, and the vintage. Some producers release Sémillon with five or more years of age as museum releases. Screw caps, standard since the 2000s, help Sémillon age freshly.

Young Sémillon suits oysters, sashimi and light seafood. Aged Sémillon suits roast chicken, crab, lobster and creamy dishes. Hunter Shiraz suits lamb, roast beef and mushrooms. Serve Sémillon at 8 to 11 degrees, Shiraz at 15 to 17. Young Sémillon is crisp; wait 10 years for its toasty magic.
Which dish suits young Hunter Sémillon?
Its lean, lemony acidity suits oysters.
Buy a few bottles of young Hunter Sémillon and open one each year. You'll taste it change from lemon to toast and honey.
Hunter Shiraz is usually very high in alcohol, like Barossa Shiraz.
Not true. It's medium-bodied, around 13 to 13.5%.
